title: Affine comparison of local dimension and both transcendence-degree terms
statement:
Let $f:X\to S$ be a dominant morphism of integral schemes [def-pc-integral-scheme], where dominant means that $f(X)$ is dense in $S$. Let $U\subseteq S$ and $V\subseteq X$ be nonempty affine opens with $f(V)\subseteq U$, put $A=\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_S)$, $B=\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_X)$, and let $\varphi:A\to B$ be the induced ring map [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. For $x\in V$ and $s=f(x)$ let $\mathfrak q\subset B$ and $\mathfrak p\subset A$ be their corresponding primes. Write $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak r)$ for the supremum of lengths of strict chains of primes ending at $\mathfrak r$; $A_{\mathfrak p},B_{\mathfrak q}$ are localizations at primes [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Then $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$, and the canonical germ isomorphisms
$$A_{\mathfrak p}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal O_{S,s},\qquad B_{\mathfrak q}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal O_{X,x}$$
intertwine the localization map induced by $\varphi$ with the stalk map of $f$ [def-weil-pbc-module-stalk]. Consequently [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring],
$$\dim\mathcal O_{S,s}=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p),\qquad\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q).$$
The quotient maps of these local rings induce field isomorphisms
$$\kappa(s)\simeq\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p)=\kappa(\mathfrak p),\qquad\kappa(x)\simeq\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak q)=\kappa(\mathfrak q)$$
which intertwine the residue-field map of $f$ with the field map induced by $\varphi$ [def-weil-residue-field]. For algebra transcendence degree [def-kun-transcendence-degree], including the $A$-algebra $B$, these identifications give
$$\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(s)}\kappa(x)=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak q),\qquad\operatorname{trdeg}_A B=\operatorname{trdeg}_{R(S)}R(X).$$
Here $R(S)=\mathcal O_{S,\eta_S}$ and $R(X)=\mathcal O_{X,\eta_X}$, for the generic points [def-sc-generic-point], and the field extension is the actual generic stalk map of $f$. No Noetherian or finite-type hypothesis is needed for these comparisons.

source.place: Tag 02JU (lemma-dimension-formula), reduction to the algebra dimension formula: the prime contraction and stalk identifications from former step 1, and all local dimension, residue-field naturality and domain-transcendence-degree comparisons from former step 2 of lem-trf-local-dimension-formula. Blueprint ancestor lem-trf-local-term-locality, proof (1)--(2), normal-cone dimension bound.

proof.text: Let $g_s:A\to\mathcal O_{S,s}$ and $g_x:B\to\mathcal O_{X,x}$ be the germ maps. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization](c) to the two given affine opens to obtain the canonical isomorphisms $e_s:A_{\mathfrak p}\simeq\mathcal O_{S,s}$ and $e_x:B_{\mathfrak q}\simeq\mathcal O_{X,x}$, with $e_s(a/t)=(g_s a)(g_s t)^{-1}$ and the analogous formula for $e_x$. Under them the maximal ideals correspond to $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ and $\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q}$. In particular $g_s^{-1}(\mathfrak m_s)=\mathfrak p$ and $g_x^{-1}(\mathfrak m_x)=\mathfrak q$: for example $a/1\in\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ iff $a\in\mathfrak p$, indeed membership gives $a/1=b/t$ with $b\in\mathfrak p$, $t\notin\mathfrak p$, so $u(ta-b)=0$ for some $u\notin\mathfrak p$; hence $uta=ub\in\mathfrak p$ and primality gives $a\in\mathfrak p$. The converse follows from $a/1$ being a generator of the extended ideal. By the definition of a morphism of locally ringed spaces, $h=f^\sharp_x$ commutes with germs, $h g_s=g_x\varphi$, and is local. Its inverse image of $\mathfrak m_x$ is $\mathfrak m_s$: it sends $\mathfrak m_s$ into $\mathfrak m_x$, while an element outside $\mathfrak m_s$ is a unit and its image is a unit. Taking inverse images in this germ square therefore gives $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$.

source.place: Tags 01HV (lemma-spec-sheaves), part (6), and 01HY (lemma-morphism-into-affine-where-point-goes), proof: the commutative germ square and localness.

proof.text:
If $t\notin\mathfrak p$, the contraction just proved gives $\varphi(t)\notin\mathfrak q$, so the map $\varphi_{\mathfrak q}:A_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}$ is $a/t\mapsto\varphi(a)/\varphi(t)$. For every such fraction the germ square gives
$$h(e_s(a/t))=h(g_sa)h(g_st)^{-1}=g_x(\varphi(a))g_x(\varphi(t))^{-1}=e_x(\varphi_{\mathfrak q}(a/t)).$$
Every element of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ has this form. Thus $h e_s=e_x\varphi_{\mathfrak q}$, proving the required naturality of the local-ring identifications.

source.place: Tag 01HY (lemma-morphism-into-affine-where-point-goes), commutative square, and Tag 01HV(6); the calculation is on fractions.

proof.text: A ring isomorphism sends prime ideals bijectively to prime ideals, preserves and reflects strict inclusion, and hence identifies their sets of chain lengths. Thus the isomorphisms in step 1 preserve Krull dimension. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-dimension-chains-below-prime], $\dim A_{\mathfrak p}$ is the supremum of chain lengths with last prime contained in $\mathfrak p$. This equals the supremum with last prime equal to $\mathfrak p$: append $\mathfrak p$ to a chain whose last prime is strictly smaller; conversely every chain ending at $\mathfrak p$ is already counted. This argument also applies when lengths are unbounded. It yields $\dim\mathcal O_{S,s}=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$; the identical argument for $B,\mathfrak q$ yields $\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)$.

source.place: Tags 00E3 (lemma-spec-localization) and 00KF (definition-height); apply the existing localization-chain comparison to both rings.

proof.text: The ring isomorphisms $e_s,e_x$ send the unique maximal ideals to one another. Passing to their quotients gives $\kappa(s)\simeq A_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and $\kappa(x)\simeq B_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q}=\kappa(\mathfrak q)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-prime-residue-field-algebra](b), these latter fields are canonically fraction fields of $A/\mathfrak p$ and $B/\mathfrak q$, respectively. The square in step 2 descends to the quotient square: on the residue of $a/t$ its map is the residue of $\varphi(a)/\varphi(t)$. This is exactly the map $\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p)\to\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak q)$ induced by the injective map $A/\mathfrak p\to B/\mathfrak q$ (injective by contraction). Thus the field identifications intertwine the actual residue-field map of $f$.

source.place: Local rings, paragraph identifying the residue field of R_p with Frac(R/p), via Tag 00CT (proposition-localize-quotient), and the following paragraph r/g maps to phi(r)/phi(g).

proof.text: The commuting field isomorphisms of step 4 preserve algebraic independence: transport each coefficient of a polynomial relation through the base-field isomorphism, and each member of the family through the extension-field isomorphism. Commutativity makes evaluation agree, and injectivity makes a nonzero polynomial remain nonzero. The inverse field isomorphisms give the converse. This bijects the algebraically independent subsets without changing their cardinalities, so their suprema give $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(s)}\kappa(x)=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak q)$.

source.place: Tag 030G (definition-transcendence-degree); apply the definition of algebraic independence under the commuting field isomorphisms.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-integral-function-field-affine-fraction] to $(S,U)$ and $(X,V)$. It gives $\eta_S\in U$, $\eta_X\in V$, domains $A,B$, and injective germ maps $i_A:A\to F=R(S)$ and $i_B:B\to L=R(X)$ making $F,L$ fraction fields. Continuity gives $f(X)=f(\overline{\{\eta_X\}})\subseteq\overline{\{f(\eta_X)\}}$; density of $f(X)$ makes $f(\eta_X)$ a generic point of $S$, hence $f(\eta_X)=\eta_S$ (uniqueness for the integral scheme, as in the cited fraction-field node). Let $j:F\to L$ be the actual generic stalk map; it is injective, since it is a unital homomorphism of fields. Compatibility of the structure-sheaf morphism with germs gives $j i_A=i_B\varphi$. Consequently $\varphi$ is injective as well: if $\varphi(a)=0$ then $j(i_A(a))=0$, and both $j$ and $i_A$ are injective. On a fraction $i_A(a)i_A(t)^{-1}$, $t\ne0$, this same germ square gives $j(i_A(a)i_A(t)^{-1})=i_B(\varphi(a))i_B(\varphi(t))^{-1}$; the denominator is nonzero by injectivity. Thus the generic field extension is the one induced by the given affine ring map. All algebra structures in the two towers $A\to B\to L$ and $A\to F\to L$ are therefore injective and have the same composite $A\to L$.

source.place: Tag 01RV (lemma-integral-scheme-rational-functions), integral case, with Schemes Tag 01HV(6) on the nonempty affine opens; generic-point image follows from continuity and dominance.

proof.text: For $z\in F$ the fraction-field description gives $z=i_A(a)i_A(t)^{-1}$ with $a,t\in A$, $t\ne0$. The nonzero polynomial $tT-a\in A[T]$ vanishes at $z$. Hence no nonempty subset of $F$ is algebraically independent over $A$ (a relation in any one member is already a relation in the full family), whereas the empty subset is independent because $i_A$ is injective. Thus $\operatorname{trdeg}_A F=0$ directly from its defining supremum. The same calculation $tT-b$ for a fraction of elements of $B$ in $L$ gives $\operatorname{trdeg}_B L=0$.

source.place: Tag 030G (definition-transcendence-degree), using the fraction representations of Morphisms Tag 01RV; the nonzero linear relations are written explicitly.

proof.text:
Use [lem-exc-domain-transcendence-degree-tower] first on $A\subseteq B\subseteq L$, and then on $A\subseteq F\subseteq L$, identifying injective maps with their images. Its hypotheses hold by step 6: every ring is a domain, all maps are injective, and both composites are the actual generic germ map. Substituting the two zeros of step 7 gives
$$\operatorname{trdeg}_A L=\operatorname{trdeg}_A B+0=\operatorname{trdeg}_A B,\qquad
\operatorname{trdeg}_A L=0+\operatorname{trdeg}_F L=\operatorname{trdeg}_{R(S)}R(X).$$
This proves the final comparison. Only adding zero is used, so the argument is valid for arbitrary infinite cardinals too. Together with steps 1--5 this proves every clause, without a Noetherian or finite-type assumption.
